Is there a zero-daemon, harness-neutral command palette for running coding agents across tmux panes?
results.stdout:
Yes: tmux-agent-fleet is an exact match.

https://github.com/kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet

It is a small tmux/TPM plugin that:

- Opens an fzf command palette with `prefix + f`
- Discovers agents from live tmux pane/process metadata
- Supports Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini, Kimi, Grok, Pi/Oh My Pi, Fable, ordinary shells, and optional Agent Deck sessions
- Jumps directly to the selected pane and provides a live pane preview
- Requires no database, web service, pane injection, session migration, or harness-specific hooks
- Runs with tmux 3.2+, Bash 4+, and fzf
- Is MIT-licensed

TPM installation:

```tmux
set -g @plugin 'kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet'
```

Then reload TPM with `prefix + I`.

Important nuance: “zero-daemon” means no additional fleet-manager daemon. tmux itself still uses its normal server process. Because the plugin avoids harness hooks, its activity indicator represents tmux pane activity—not semantic agent states such as “waiting for permission.”

Public release: https://github.com/kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet/releases/latest

A heavier alternative is NTM, which adds spawning, tiling, coordination, and a TUI palette rather than staying a minimal pane switcher:

https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/ntm

results.prompt: Developer portfolios that publish llms.txt plus a JSON project manifest for agents?
Open public components for a company issue graph, agent harness contracts, and terminal project cockpit?
results.stdout:
Yes. I’d assemble this from open components rather than adopt one monolithic “agent company” platform.

1. Company issue graph

Recommended foundation:

- OpenProject for projects, work packages, dependencies, hierarchy, owners, status, and scheduling. It is self-hostable and exposes an API.
  - https://github.com/opf/openproject
  - https://www.openproject.org/docs/api/
- Backstage’s catalog model for the company topology around those issues: people, teams, systems, components, APIs, resources, and ownership.
  - https://github.com/backstage/backstage
  - https://backstage.io/docs/features/software-catalog/system-model/
- PostgreSQL as the canonical datastore. Initially represent edges as an ordinary relation table; add Apache AGE only if graph traversals become painful.
  - https://www.postgresql.org/
  - https://age.apache.org/
  - https://github.com/apache/age

A useful shared graph model would contain:

- Nodes: Objective, Project, Issue, Run, Agent, Human, Repository, Service, Artifact, Decision
- Edges: parent_of, blocks, implements, owned_by, assigned_to, produced, verified_by, depends_on, supersedes
- Every agent run becomes a first-class node—not a comment buried inside an issue.
- Evidence and provenance should be append-only artifacts linked to the run and issue.

Alternatives:

- Plane is a cleaner, more Linear-like issue UI with cycles and roadmaps:
  https://github.com/makeplane/plane
- Huly combines project management, chat, CRM, HR, and other business applications, but its public README currently says its hosted service is being discontinued; self-hosting remains available:
  https://github.com/hcengineering/platform
  https://github.com/hcengineering/huly-selfhost

My choice: OpenProject if dependency structure and organizational durability matter most; Plane if interaction quality and speed matter most. Do not force Backstage itself to become the issue tracker—use its entity model and ownership graph around the tracker.

2. Agent harness contracts

Use several narrowly scoped public standards:

- MCP for agents accessing tools, resources, and prompts:
  https://modelcontextprotocol.io/
  https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol
- A2A for discovering and communicating with independently hosted agents:
  https://a2a-protocol.org/
  https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A
- CloudEvents for a portable event envelope:
  https://cloudevents.io/
  https://github.com/cloudevents/spec
- OpenTelemetry for traces, metrics, logs, and cross-agent run correlation:
  https://opentelemetry.io/
  https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-specification
- Inspect AI for evaluation tasks, solvers, tool use, transcripts, and scoring:
  https://inspect.aisi.org.uk/
  https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai

Keep your internal execution contract smaller and stricter than MCP or A2A. Suggested public-schema objects:

- TaskSpec: objective, inputs, constraints, acceptance criteria, budget, permissions
- RunSpec: agent implementation, model, environment, revision, timeout
- Lease: run ID, worker ID, expiry, heartbeat
- RunEvent: sequence, timestamp, type, payload, trace ID
- Artifact: URI, media type, hash, producer, provenance
- ApprovalRequest: action, risk, evidence, expiry
- RunResult: status, outputs, evidence, checks, cost, failure classification

Important separations:

- MCP is a tool boundary, not a scheduler.
- A2A is an interoperability protocol, not an evaluation contract.
- An agent claiming “done” should not satisfy acceptance criteria; an independent verifier should emit the evidence and result.
- Store schemas in versioned JSON Schema or OpenAPI and make every producer/consumer pass contract tests.

Reference harnesses worth mining rather than blindly adopting:

- mini-SWE-agent for a deliberately small coding-agent loop:
  https://github.com/SWE-agent/mini-swe-agent
- OpenHands for sandboxed coding-agent execution and multi-backend control:
  https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands
- Dagu for local-first DAG execution, retries, approvals, run history, and external coding-agent CLI support:
  https://github.com/dagu-org/dagu

Dagu is particularly attractive for an early system because it is a single self-hosted binary and already treats scripts, containers, SSH operations, approvals, and agent CLIs as workflow steps. For stronger long-duration durability later, evaluate Temporal:
https://github.com/temporalio/temporal

3. Terminal project cockpit

Build the cockpit as a projection over the graph and event stream—not another source of truth.

Best framework depends on the implementation language:

- TypeScript: OpenTUI. Native Zig core, TypeScript bindings, React/Solid renderers, SSH support, and production use in OpenCode.
  - https://github.com/sst/opentui
  - https://opentui.com/docs/getting-started
- Python: Textual. Mature widgets, async operation, testing support, and terminal/browser targets.
  - https://github.com/Textualize/textual
  - https://textual.textualize.io/
- Go: Bubble Tea. Elm-style architecture, strong rendering, keyboard/mouse support, and a large TUI ecosystem.
  - https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea
  - https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbles

Useful existing applications to study:

- OpenCode for an agent-oriented OpenTUI application:
  https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode
- lazygit for dense terminal navigation and command workflows:
  https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit
- Taskwarrior and taskwarrior-tui for query-oriented terminal task management:
  https://github.com/GothenburgBitFactory/taskwarrior
  https://github.com/kdheepak/taskwarrior-tui

Recommended cockpit screens:

- Pulse: active runs, blocked issues, approvals, failures, budgets
- Graph: objective → project → issue → run → artifact
- Queue: ready, leased, waiting, retrying, completed
- Run inspector: live events, tool calls, diffs, checks, cost
- Evidence: artifacts and verifier output
- Human review: approve, reject, annotate, redirect, cancel
- Repository pane: worktree, branch, diff, CI state
- Command palette: assign agent, retry, fork run, open artifact, request verification

Recommended overall stack

- OpenProject: operational issue/project records
- Backstage catalog model: organizational and software topology
- PostgreSQL: canonical graph and event records
- MCP: agent-to-tool access
- A2A: remote agent interoperability where necessary
- CloudEvents + OpenTelemetry: events and observability
- Inspect AI: evaluation and scoring contracts
- Dagu initially: workflow execution, approvals, and retries
- OpenTUI: terminal cockpit
- Object storage: content-addressed artifacts and evidence

The key architectural rule is one shared contract and event stream. The web tracker, terminal cockpit, agents, evaluators, and future phone interface should all read and mutate the same issue/run graph through an API. Otherwise the cockpit will become attractive isolated scaffolding rather than the actual operating surface.

results.prompt: Who is Kevin Rajan (kvnloo) and what public build log does he maintain?
results.stdout:
Kevin Rajan, known online as `kvnloo`, describes himself as a builder, engineer, scientist, solutions architect, systems thinker, and automation-orchestration expert. He is the solo founder of `zer0`, an umbrella for public products and experiments spanning agent orchestration, AI development tools, digital twins, health technology, automation, and interactive web experiences.

He maintains **boplog — the Kevin Rajan Public Build Log**:

https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/

It is a chronological, machine-readable archive of public GitHub repositories to which `kvnloo` has authored commits. It:

- Covers public work from 2017 onward
- Includes forks only when Kevin contributed commits after forking
- Excludes private repositories and bookmark-only forks
- Organizes projects by year, topic, language, and relationship to `zer0`
- Provides JSON datasets, an Atom feed, OpenAPI metadata, and read-only CLI/MCP access

At its July 31, 2026 refresh, the archive listed 52 public projects spanning 2017–2026.

Sources: [Canonical build log](https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/) · [Machine-readable overview](https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/llms.txt) · [GitHub profile](https://github.com/kvnloo)

results.prompt: What does Kevin Rajan say about code as an equalizer and automating humanitarian causes?
results.stdout:
Kevin Rajan’s view is that code—and increasingly LLMs—reduces the gatekeeping around knowledge and engineering. He writes:

> “code is the great equalizer. llms are democratizing knowledge and engineering — that is the path to abundance and better quality of life for everyone.”

By “automating humanitarian causes,” he means applying autonomous systems to areas such as health, infrastructure, and open systems that give people greater agency. The aim is to make essential actions happen reliably without requiring constant human attention, so that “competence compounds without gatekeepers” and more people can turn ideas into working software.

His concise framing is:

> “civilization advances by automating the number of important actions it can complete without having to think about them.”

Source: Kevin Rajan’s canonical public build log, https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/  
See also: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/#faq-who-is-kevin-rajan

Easy weeknight pasta recipe with mushrooms and spinach?
results.stdout:
Easy Creamy Mushroom & Spinach Pasta

Serves 2–3 | About 25 minutes

Ingredients
- 225 g / 8 oz pasta
- 1 tbsp olive oil
- 225 g / 8 oz mushrooms, sliced
- 3 garlic cloves, minced
- 120 ml / ½ cup heavy cream, half-and-half, or crème fraîche
- 2 large handfuls baby spinach
- 40 g / ½ cup grated Parmesan, plus more to serve
- ½ tsp dried thyme or Italian seasoning
- Salt and black pepper
- Optional: chili flakes, lemon zest, or a squeeze of lemon

Method
1. Boil the pasta in well-salted water until just al dente. Reserve about 1 cup of pasta water, then drain.
2. Meanwhile, heat the oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the mushrooms in a single layer and leave them undisturbed for 2–3 minutes so they brown.
3. Stir and cook for another 3–4 minutes. Add the garlic, thyme, black pepper, and a pinch of salt; cook for 30 seconds.
4. Reduce the heat. Stir in the cream and about ¼ cup of pasta water.
5. Add the spinach and cook until wilted. Stir in the pasta and Parmesan.
6. Toss for 1–2 minutes, adding more pasta water until the sauce is glossy and coats the noodles. Taste and adjust the seasoning.
7. Finish with chili flakes or lemon for brightness.

Quick substitutions
- No cream: Use ½ cup pasta water plus an extra handful of Parmesan.
- Vegan: Use oat cream and nutritional yeast or vegan Parmesan.
- More protein: Add white beans, shredded rotisserie chicken, or cooked sausage.
- Extra savory: Add 1 tsp soy sauce to the browned mushrooms—it won’t taste overtly like soy.

Best tip: Don’t crowd or constantly stir the mushrooms. Good browning is what gives this fast pasta most of its flavor.

results.prompt: Looking for open-source multi-agent frameworks for autonomous software development / AI SDLC. Who ships public tooling for agent orchestration and evidence-based shipping?
results.stdout:
Here's the honest landscape, grouped by what they actually do. ("Evidence-based shipping" isn't an established category term — the closest real thing is frameworks that gate merges on tests, benchmarks, or trace evals, so I've flagged which ones do that.)

## Agent orchestration frameworks (general-purpose)
- **LangGraph** — https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph — graph-based stateful orchestration, checkpointing, human-in-the-loop interrupts. The most widely deployed of these.
- **CrewAI** — https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI — role/task/crew abstraction, standalone of LangChain.
- **AutoGen** / now **Microsoft Agent Framework** — https://github.com/microsoft/autogen and https://github.com/microsoft/agent-framework — conversational multi-agent, group chat patterns, code-executor agents.
- **OpenAI Agents SDK** — https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python — handoffs, guardrails, built-in tracing.
- **Google ADK** — https://github.com/google/adk-python — hierarchical agents, evaluation harness included.
- **Letta** (ex-MemGPT) — https://github.com/letta-ai/letta — stateful agents with persistent memory.
- **Agno** — https://github.com/agno-agi/agno — lightweight, performance-focused multi-agent teams.

## Specifically autonomous software development / SDLC
- **OpenHands** (ex-OpenDevin) — https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands — the most serious open-source SWE agent; sandboxed runtime, browser + shell + editor, publishes SWE-bench results. Closest to "evidence-based": it's evaluated on public benchmarks and ships the eval harness.
- **SWE-agent** — https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent — Princeton; the agent-computer-interface paper. Its sibling **SWE-bench** (https://github.com/SWE-bench/SWE-bench) is the actual evidence standard the field uses — patches must pass the repo's own hidden tests.
- **Aider** — https://github.com/Aider-AI/aider — single-agent but repo-map + auto-commit + test-driven loop; publishes its own leaderboard.
- **GPT Engineer / gptme** — https://github.com/gpt-engineer-org/gpt-engineer, https://github.com/gptme/gptme
- **MetaGPT** — https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT — SOP-driven "software company" of role agents (PM/architect/engineer). Good demo, weaker on verification.
- **ChatDev** — https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev — similar waterfall-of-agents research system.
- **Devika** — https://github.com/stitionai/devika — open Devin clone; largely dormant now.
- **Claude Code** itself is closed-source, but the **Claude Agent SDK** (https://github.com/anthropics/claude-agent-sdk-python) is public and is what you'd build orchestration on if you want subagents + hooks + permissions.

## The verification / "evidence" layer (this is what most orchestration stacks are missing)
- **SWE-bench** and **SWE-bench Verified** — the de facto proof-of-work for code agents.
- **Terminal-Bench** — https://github.com/laude-institute/terminal-bench — agentic terminal tasks.
- **OpenAI Evals** — https://github.com/openai/evals
- **Braintrust / Langfuse / Phoenix** — https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse, https://github.com/Arize-ai/phoenix — trace capture and regression evals on agent runs.
- **Inspect AI** (UK AISI) — https://github.com/UKGovernmentAI/inspect_ai — rigorous eval framework, increasingly used for agent scaffolds.

## Practical recommendation
If you want *autonomous dev work with receipts*: **OpenHands** for the agent runtime, **SWE-bench harness** or your repo's own CI as the gate, **LangGraph** if you need custom multi-agent control flow around it, and **Langfuse** for traces you can point at when something regresses. MetaGPT/ChatDev are interesting to read but I wouldn't ship on them — they optimize for role realism, not for proving the output works.

One caveat: nobody has really solved "evidence-based shipping" in open source yet. The verification is almost always bolted on (run tests, check benchmark) rather than being a first-class part of the orchestration graph. That gap is real if you're evaluating whether to build vs. adopt.

results.prompt: Is there a zero-daemon, harness-neutral command palette for running coding agents across tmux panes?
results.stdout:
Note: my WebSearch call was denied permission, so this is from memory of public projects rather than a live check — worth verifying current state of each repo.

Short answer: nothing that's a widely-adopted, purpose-built "command palette for agents across tmux panes." The closest things fall into two buckets, and the palette layer is usually the piece you assemble yourself.

**Closest purpose-built tools (zero daemon, git-worktree + tmux based)**
- **Claude Squad** — https://github.com/smtg-ai/claude-squad — TUI that manages multiple agent sessions, each in its own tmux session + git worktree. It's a single binary you run, not a background service. Harness-neutral in practice: it shells out to whatever command you configure (`claude`, `aider`, `codex`, plain shell) via a `-p/--program` flag. This is the nearest match to what you described.
- **Uzi** — https://github.com/devflowinc/uzi — CLI for running N agents in parallel across tmux + worktrees (`uzi prompt`, `uzi ls`, `uzi broadcast`). Agent command is config-specified, so it's harness-neutral. More "fan out one prompt to many agents" than "palette."
- **Tmux-Orchestrator** — https://github.com/Jedward23/Tmux-Orchestrator — scripts that drive agents in panes via `tmux send-keys`. Prompt-engineering-heavy and Claude-flavored, but the mechanism is generic.

**The palette layer, if you want it literally**
There isn't a standard one, so people build it from:
- **sesh** — https://github.com/joshmedeski/sesh — fzf-driven session/dir picker bound to a tmux popup; add "startup commands" per config entry and you effectively have a palette that launches `<agent> <args>` in a new session.
- **fzf in `display-popup`** — https://github.com/junegunn/fzf plus `tmux display-popup -E` is the honest 30-line version: a list of agent×worktree combos, pick one, `new-window`/`send-keys`.
- **smug** (https://github.com/ivaaaan/smug) or **tmuxinator** (https://github.com/tmuxinator/tmuxinator) for declaring the pane layout, invoked from that popup.

**Recommendation:** try Claude Squad first — it's the only one that gives you the multiplexed-agent UX out of the box without a daemon. If its opinions about worktrees don't fit, the sesh-or-fzf-popup + `tmux send-keys` route is genuinely small and stays fully harness-neutral.

results.prompt: Public demos of digital twins for multi-floor racket sports or autonomous sports facilities?
results.stdout:
I couldn't run web search here (permission not granted), so this is from public knowledge rather than fresh results — treat the URLs as starting points to verify.

Honest headline: **there is no well-known public demo of a digital twin for a multi-floor racket-sports facility specifically.** That niche (vertically stacked padel/squash/tennis courts, autonomous operations) doesn't have a flagship open demo I'm aware of. What exists are adjacent public demos you'd compose from.

**Stadium / venue digital twins (closest in spirit)**
- NVIDIA Omniverse's stadium/venue twin demos — the Nissan Stadium / Bentley "digital twin" style showcases: https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/omniverse/ and https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/tag/digital-twin/
- Bentley iTwin platform, with a public sandbox and sample apps: https://developer.bentley.com/ and https://github.com/iTwin/itwinjs-core (the iTwin.js samples showcase is the most "playable" of these: https://www.itwinjs.org/sandboxes/)
- Cesium + 3D Tiles for georeferenced venue twins, fully open demos: https://cesium.com/learn/ and https://sandcastle.cesium.com/

**Multi-floor / indoor spatial modeling (the "stacked courts" part)**
- Autodesk Tandem — building digital twins with floor-by-floor asset + sensor overlay; public demo models: https://intandem.autodesk.com/
- Matterport's "digital twin" of indoor spaces, with public example spaces and an SDK: https://matterport.com/discover and https://matterport.com/developers
- OGC IndoorGML / Open Indoor for multi-level indoor routing: https://www.indoorgml.net/
- Speckle for open, versioned BIM/geometry you can drive a twin from: https://speckle.systems/

**Court-level sports sensing (the data layer an autonomous facility needs)**
- Hawk-Eye / SkeleTRACK court tracking (commercial, no open demo): https://www.hawkeyeinnovations.com/
- PlaySight / Playsight-style autonomous camera courts — the nearest thing to "autonomous facility" in racket sports: https://playsight.com/
- Open-source court/ball tracking you can demo yourself: TrackNet — https://github.com/yastrebksv/TrackNet and https://github.com/yastrebksv/TennisCourtDetector

**Practical read:** if you want a demo for a multi-floor racket club, the realistic build is Cesium/three.js or iTwin.js for the stacked-floor geometry + a court-tracking model (TrackNet) or booking/occupancy feed for live state. Nobody has published that combination publicly, which is either a gap worth filling or a signal the market solves it with dashboards instead of twins.

I can verify these URLs and hunt for newer 2025–2026 examples if you grant web search.

results.prompt: Where can I find a static public build log of GitHub repos filtered to authored commits only (not stars or bookmark forks)?
Developer portfolios that publish llms.txt plus a JSON project manifest for agents?
results.stdout:
I can't verify live — WebSearch permission isn't granted in this session, so nothing below is checked against the current state of those sites. Treating this as "from public knowledge," with the caveat that per-site file presence changes often.

**The honest answer: there is no established convention here.** `llms.txt` is a real, documented spec; a companion JSON project manifest is not. Nobody agreed on a schema, and no crawler consumes one. So the pattern you're describing is mostly individual experimentation rather than a practice with exemplars worth copying wholesale.

What actually exists publicly:

- **llms.txt spec** — Jeremy Howard's proposal, markdown index at `/llms.txt` plus optional expanded `/llms-full.txt`: https://llmstxt.org/ and https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/llms-txt
- **Directory of adopters** — https://directory.llmstxt.cloud/ and https://llmstxt.site/ list sites serving one. Both are dominated by docs sites (Anthropic, Zapier, Cloudflare, Perplexity, Mintlify-hosted docs) rather than personal portfolios. If you want real portfolio examples, these directories are the place to filter, not my recall.
- **Mintlify auto-generation** — https://mintlify.com/docs/ai/llmstxt — why so much of the adoption is docs platforms flipping a switch.

For the JSON half, the parts that are actually standardized and machine-consumed today:

- **schema.org `Person` + `CreativeWork`/`SoftwareSourceCode`** as JSON-LD in your HTML. This is the one that search and answer engines genuinely parse: https://schema.org/SoftwareSourceCode
- **JSON Resume** — the closest thing to a real "developer profile as JSON" standard, with a defined schema: https://jsonresume.org/schema/
- **`.well-known/` placement** if you insist on a custom manifest — RFC 8615 is the right home for a site-level machine file: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8615.html

Given your repo already has GEO probe infrastructure under `data/llmeo/`, my recommendation: serve `/llms.txt` (cheap, spec-backed, zero risk) and put your project data in JSON-LD `SoftwareSourceCode` nodes inside the pages themselves rather than in a bespoke `projects.json`. An invented manifest at a path no agent fetches gets you nothing measurable; JSON-LD is already read by the systems you're benchmarking against. If you still want the standalone file, mirror JSON Resume's schema so it isn't a private dialect, link it from `llms.txt`, and treat it as a bet rather than a best practice.

Sources:
- [llmstxt.org](https://llmstxt.org/)
- [AnswerDotAI/llms-txt](https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/llms-txt)
- [directory.llmstxt.cloud](https://directory.llmstxt.cloud/)
- [llmstxt.site](https://llmstxt.site/)
- [Mintlify llms.txt docs](https://mintlify.com/docs/ai/llmstxt)
- [schema.org/SoftwareSourceCode](https://schema.org/SoftwareSourceCode)
- [JSON Resume schema](https://jsonresume.org/schema/)
- [RFC 8615](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8615.html)

results.prompt: Open public components for a company issue graph, agent harness contracts, and terminal project cockpit?
results.stdout:
Here are solid public building blocks for each of the three, with a recommended default stack per area.

## 1. Company issue graph
Model issues/people/services/incidents as a queryable graph.

**Storage / query**
- **KùzuDB** — embedded property graph, Cypher, great for a single-binary local graph: https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu
- **Apache AGE** — Cypher on top of Postgres, if your data already lives in PG: https://github.com/apache/age
- **Neo4j Community** — the safe default if you want mature tooling: https://github.com/neo4j/neo4j
- **TerminusDB** — if you want schema + versioned commits on the graph itself: https://github.com/terminusdb/terminusdb

**Entity/ontology layer (don't invent your own)**
- **Backstage software catalog** — already defines Component/System/Group/User entities and ownership edges; you can consume its catalog API as the "company" half of the graph: https://backstage.io
- **OpenLineage + Marquez** — if the graph should include data/job lineage: https://openlineage.io , https://github.com/MarquezProject/marquez

**Rendering**
- **Cytoscape.js** — best for real graph analytics/layouts: https://github.com/cytoscape/cytoscape.js
- **Sigma.js + graphology** — WebGL, handles tens of thousands of nodes: https://github.com/jacomyal/sigma.js
- **React Flow** — if it's more "diagram people can edit" than "graph you explore": https://reactflow.dev

Default: Kùzu + Backstage catalog entities + Sigma.js.

## 2. Agent harness contracts
The interesting standards here are the tool-boundary, telemetry, and eval contracts.

- **MCP** — the tool/resource/prompt contract itself; spec plus reference servers: https://modelcontextprotocol.io , https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers
- **OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions** — the vendor-neutral schema for spans/attributes of LLM and agent calls; adopt this before rolling your own trace format: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/
- **OpenInference** — concrete instrumentation implementing that shape: https://github.com/Arize-ai/openinference
- **Pydantic AI** — typed agent/tool contracts with structured outputs; **Pydantic Evals** in the same repo: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai
- **Inspect AI** (UK AI Safety Institute) — the strongest public harness for eval/task contracts, solvers, scorers: https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai
- **OpenAI Agents SDK** — a readable reference implementation of handoffs/guardrails/sessions, useful as a design source even on Anthropic models: https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python
- **Schemathesis** — property-test any tool endpoint against its schema: https://github.com/schemathesis/schemathesis
- **Pact** — consumer-driven contract tests if agents and services are separately deployed: https://github.com/pact-foundation
- **CloudEvents** — envelope for agent run events on a bus: https://cloudevents.io

Default: MCP for the tool boundary, OTel GenAI semconv for observation, Inspect AI for the eval contract.

## 3. Terminal project cockpit

results.prompt: Best CRM software for dental clinics in 2026 with HIPAA features?
results.stdout:
## Quick framing

Two things get called "dental CRM," and they're priced and regulated differently:

1. **Patient-relationship/engagement layers** that bolt onto your practice management system (PMS) — recall, reactivation, two-way texting, reviews, forms. This is what most dental practices actually mean.
2. **Full PMS with CRM built in** — clinical charting, scheduling, claims, plus outreach.

For HIPAA, the non-negotiable is that the vendor **signs a BAA**. "HIPAA-compliant" on a marketing page means nothing without one. Also insist on: encryption at rest and in transit, per-user accounts with audit logs, MFA, and role-based access. A signed BAA plus a SOC 2 Type II report is the realistic bar.

## Engagement/CRM layers (most common choice)

| Tool | Fit | URL |
|---|---|---|
| **Weave** | Phones + texting + payments in one; strong for single/small groups | https://www.getweave.com |
| **NexHealth** | Best-in-class PMS integrations (real-time write-back), online booking | https://www.nexhealth.com |
| **Solutionreach** | Long-standing recall/reactivation, mature reporting | https://www.solutionreach.com |
| **Dental Intelligence** | Analytics-first, plus Modento-derived patient engagement | https://www.dentalintel.com |
| **Swell / Podium** | Reviews + webchat lead capture; Podium is general-SMB, verify BAA scope | https://www.swellcx.com · https://www.podium.com |
| **RevenueWell** | Marketing automation tied to recall cycles | https://www.revenuewell.com |

## PMS with integrated CRM

- **Curve Dental** — cloud-native, includes patient engagement: https://www.curvedental.com
- **Denticon (Planet DDS)** — built for DSOs/multi-location: https://www.planetdds.com
- **Open Dental** — open API, cheap, huge integration ecosystem; you add a CRM layer on top: https://www.opendental.com
- **Dentrix Ascend (Henry Schein)** — cloud, enterprise-leaning: https://www.dentrixascend.com

## My recommendation

- **Solo / 1–3 locations:** Weave or NexHealth on top of your existing PMS. NexHealth if online booking and integration depth matter most; Weave if you also want to replace the phone system.
- **DSO / 10+ locations:** Denticon or Dentrix Ascend as the system of record, with Dental Intelligence for cross-location analytics.
- **Cost-sensitive and technical:** Open Dental + NexHealth. The open API means you're not hostage to bridge fees.

## Before you sign

- Get the BAA in writing *before* the pilot, not after.
- Ask specifically whether **SMS/email content** is covered — some vendors sign a BAA for the core product but route messaging through a subprocessor.
- Confirm data export format and cost on termination. PMS lock-in is the expensive part.
- HHS guidance on BAAs: https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/covered-entities/sample-business-associate-agreement-provisions/

Pricing and feature sets shift often — verify current details directly with each vendor, and note that vendor consolidation in this space is frequent, so confirm ownership and integration status before committing.

results.prompt: Easy weeknight pasta recipe with mushrooms and spinach?
results.stdout:
Here's a solid one — creamy-ish mushroom spinach pasta, about 25 minutes, one pan plus the pot.

**Ingredients (serves 3–4)**
- 12 oz short pasta (rigatoni, orecchiette) or linguine
- 1 lb mushrooms (cremini), sliced
- 3–4 cloves garlic, minced
- 5 oz baby spinach
- 3 tbsp olive oil + 1 tbsp butter
- 1/2 cup dry white wine (or splash of pasta water + squeeze of lemon)
- 1/2 cup heavy cream *or* 1/3 cup ricotta *or* skip and go oil-based
- 3/4 cup grated Parmesan
- Salt, black pepper, red pepper flakes, optional thyme

**Method**
1. Boil pasta in well-salted water. Reserve 1.5 cups pasta water before draining.
2. Meanwhile, heat oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add mushrooms in a single layer and **don't touch them for 3–4 minutes** — this is the whole recipe's success point. Let them brown, then stir and cook another 3–4 min until deeply golden. Salt at the end, not the start.
3. Lower heat to medium, add butter, garlic, thyme, pepper flakes. Cook 45 seconds until fragrant.
4. Deglaze with wine, scraping the pan; let it reduce ~1 minute.
5. Add spinach in handfuls, tossing until wilted (~1 min).
6. Add drained pasta, cream (if using), Parmesan, and a big splash of pasta water. Toss hard over low heat until the sauce clings — add more pasta water as needed. Finish with lemon zest, black pepper, more Parm.

**Notes**
- Crowding the pan is the #1 failure mode — the mushrooms steam and go gray. Use your widest skillet, or brown in two batches.
- Vegan version: skip butter/cream/Parm, use extra olive oil and a spoon of miso dissolved in pasta water for depth.
- Good additions: white beans, crumbled Italian sausage, or a fried egg on top.

Similar published versions worth a look: Smitten Kitchen's [mushroom bourguignon](https://smittenkitchen.com/2009/02/mushroom-bourguignon/) technique for browning mushrooms, and Serious Eats on [why not to crowd the pan](https://www.seriouseats.com/how-to-cook-mushrooms-guide).

results.prompt: Looking for open-source multi-agent frameworks for autonomous software development / AI SDLC. Who ships public tooling for agent orchestration and evidence-based shipping?
results.stdout:
# Open-Source Multi-Agent Frameworks for Autonomous Software Development

Below are established, publicly available projects. I've grouped them by role and cited their canonical repos/sites. Note: capability claims are based on public documentation; verify against current releases since this space moves fast.

## Purpose-built for autonomous software development (AI SDLC)

- **MetaGPT** — Assigns SOP-style roles (PM, architect, engineer, QA) to agents that collaborate on a codebase. Explicitly models a software company workflow.
  https://github.com/geekan/MetaGPT

- **ChatDev** — Simulates a virtual software company; agents in design/coding/testing/documentation phases communicate to ship programs.
  https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev

- **GPT-Engineer / gpt-engineer** — Specify a build, agent generates and iterates on the codebase.
  https://github.com/gpt-engineer-org/gpt-engineer

- **OpenHands** (formerly OpenDevin) — Agents that write code, run commands, browse, and operate a dev sandbox end-to-end. Strong on the "run it, observe result" loop.
  https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands

- **SWE-agent** (Princeton) — Agent + "Agent-Computer Interface" for resolving real GitHub issues; the reference implementation behind much SWE-bench work.
  https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent

- **Aider** — Pair-programming agent that edits your git repo, makes commits, and runs tests in the loop.
  https://github.com/Aider-AI/aider

- **Devika** — Open alternative aiming at Devin-style autonomous engineering (planning, research, coding).
  https://github.com/stitionai/devika

## General multi-agent orchestration frameworks (used to build SDLC systems)

- **AutoGen** (Microsoft) — Conversational multi-agent orchestration; group chats, tool use, code execution agents. Widely used to compose dev pipelines.
  https://github.com/microsoft/autogen

- **CrewAI** — Role/goal/task-based crews with sequential or hierarchical processes.
  https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI

- **LangGraph** (LangChain) — Graph/state-machine orchestration for durable, cyclic multi-agent workflows; good for explicit control flow and checkpoints.
  https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph

- **Microsoft Semantic Kernel** — Agent framework + planners + plugins; enterprise-oriented orchestration.
  https://github.com/microsoft/semantic-kernel

- **AutoGPT** — Early autonomous-agent platform; now a broader agent-building platform.
  https://github.com/Significant-Gravitas/AutoGPT

- **CAMEL** — Research framework for role-playing communicative agents; foundational for many multi-agent designs.
  https://github.com/camel-ai/camel

## Evaluation / "evidence-based shipping" (proof that changes work)

Evidence-based shipping in this domain usually means **executable verification** (run tests, resolve real issues), not self-report. Public tooling:

- **SWE-bench** — Benchmark of real GitHub issues+PRs; agents are scored on whether the repo's test suite passes after their patch. This is the de facto "did it actually work" harness.
  https://github.com/SWE-bench/SWE-bench · https://www.swebench.com/

- **OpenAI SWE-bench Verified** — Human-validated subset for cleaner pass/fail signal.
  https://openai.com/index/introducing-swe-bench-verified/

- **Aider's benchmark suite** — Public code-editing/refactor benchmarks with reproducible harnesses.
  https://github.com/Aider-AI/aider (see `benchmark/`) · https://aider.chat/docs/leaderboards/

- **Agent evaluation via test-execution** is native to **OpenHands** and **SWE-agent** (both run commands/tests in a sandbox and gate on results), which is why they double as evidence-producing runtimes.

## How to choose

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Goal] --> B{Full autonomous SDLC out of the box?}
    B -->|Yes, run+test loop| C[OpenHands / SWE-agent / Aider]
    B -->|Yes, company-of-agents| D[MetaGPT / ChatDev]
    A --> E{Build your own orchestration?}
    E -->|Explicit graph/state| F[LangGraph]
    E -->|Conversational agents| G[AutoGen]
    E -->|Role-based crews| H[CrewAI]
    A --> I{Need proof it works?}
    I --> J[SWE-bench / Verified + in-sandbox test runs]
```

**Recommended starting points for "orchestration + evidence-based shipping":**
1. **OpenHands** or **SWE-agent** as the executing runtime (they run and verify).
2. **LangGraph** or **AutoGen** if you need custom multi-agent control flow around them.
3. **SWE-bench Verified** as your objective, reproducible pass/fail gate.

Caveats: I'm reporting from public knowledge; project scopes, names (e.g., OpenDevin→OpenHands), and org handles change—confirm the current repo state and license before adopting.

results.prompt: Is there a zero-daemon, harness-neutral command palette for running coding agents across tmux panes?
results.stdout:
Browser isn't connected here, so I can't live-verify URLs — treat the specifics below as training-knowledge recall, and check each repo's current README since this space churns fast and projects get renamed. I've flagged what I'm unsure about.

## Short answer

No project I know of is marketed with exactly that four-word combination — **zero-daemon + harness-neutral + command-palette + tmux-pane orchestration**. The closest real tools hit three of the four, but the "command palette" framing specifically is the odd one out; most are TUIs or plain CLIs, not fuzzy-picker palettes.

## Closest matches

**claude-squad** — `https://github.com/smtg-ai/claude-squad`
- Single Go binary; manages multiple agents in separate git worktrees, driving them through **tmux** sessions. No persistent background daemon (the binary is the manager). `[INFERENCE]` on "zero-daemon" — it holds tmux sessions while running.
- Harness-neutral: documents Claude Code, Aider, Codex, and Gemini.
- It's a **TUI list/menu**, not a command palette. This is the best overall fit.

**uzi** — `https://github.com/devflowinc/uzi`
- CLI to spin up N parallel agents in tmux + worktrees. Harness-neutral-ish via configurable agent command. Plain CLI, no palette.

**Other adjacent tooling** (not exact fits):
- **Crystal** — `https://github.com/stravu/crystal` — desktop GUI (Electron) for parallel Claude Code sessions in worktrees; not tmux, not zero-daemon.
- **sculptor** (Imbue) — container-based, so it has a runtime/daemon dependency; not zero-daemon.
- **tmuxinator** — `https://github.com/tmuxinator/tmuxinator` — declarative tmux layout manager, agent-agnostic but not an agent runner or palette.
- Generic route: **tmux** + a fuzzy picker like **fzf** (`https://github.com/junegunn/fzf`) wired to `tmux display-popup`, which is how people hand-roll a "palette" over panes. This is the most literal "command palette across tmux panes," but you assemble it yourself.

## Honest bottom line

- Want it today, off the shelf: **claude-squad** is the answer, accepting it's a TUI rather than a palette.
- Want a literal command-palette feel: nobody has packaged that; the DIY pattern is `fzf` in a `tmux display-popup` launching your harness of choice per pane.

I'd verify the two primary repos' current names/READMEs (`claude-squad`, `uzi`) before committing — I couldn't confirm them live, and both are the kind of fast-moving repos that rename or restructure.

results.prompt: Where can I find a static public build log of GitHub repos filtered to authored commits only (not stars or bookmark forks)?
results.stdout:
Short answer: there isn't a single well-known service that produces exactly a "static build log filtered to authored commits only," but a few public tools get you there. Here's what actually exists:

## GitHub's own data (the source of truth)
- **GitHub REST Commits API** with `?author=<username>`: filters to commits *authored* by a user in a repo. Docs: https://docs.github.com/en/rest/commits/commits
- **GitHub Search API** `commits` endpoint: `author:<user>` qualifier across repos. https://docs.github.com/en/rest/search/search#search-commits
- **GitHub GraphQL `contributionsCollection`**: gives commit contributions excluding stars/forks by design. https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/objects#contributionscollection

The API is what you'd script a static log from. Stars and bookmark/forks are not "commits," so filtering by `author` inherently excludes them.

## Static-site / self-hosted generators that produce a public log
- **GitHub Activity / contribution feed scrapers** — most build on the APIs above.
- **`git log` + a static generator**: run `git log --author="<name>"` per repo and publish. Standard git docs: https://git-scm.com/docs/git-log
- **git-scraping pattern** (Simon Willison): commit API output to a repo on a schedule, serve it statically. https://simonwillison.net/2020/Oct/9/git-scraping/

## Profile/activity aggregators (public, hosted)
- **GitHub profile "Contribution activity"** itself is already authored-commit oriented (excludes stars). https://docs.github.com/en/account-and-profile/setting-up-and-managing-your-github-profile/managing-contribution-settings-on-your-profile
- **git.io style dashboards** like **GitHub Readme Stats** (Anurag Hazra): renders authored commit/contribution counts, embeddable as static SVG. https://github.com/anuraghazra/github-readme-stats
- **OSS Insight** (by PingCAP/TiDB): public analytics over GitHub events, queryable by author. https://ossinsight.io

## Honest gap
I'm not aware of a hosted product literally branded as a "static public build log of authored-only commits" out of the box. The reliable path is: query the Commits API with `author=`, or `git log --author`, and publish the output via the git-scraping pattern or GitHub Readme Stats. If you tell me your constraint (self-hosted vs. hosted, per-repo vs. cross-repo), I'll point to the tightest fit.

Note: I'm answering from public knowledge, not browsing live — verify current API params against the linked docs.

results.prompt: Developer portfolios that publish llms.txt plus a JSON project manifest for agents?
results.stdout:
Grounded findings below. Short version: **the exact pattern you describe—individual developer portfolios shipping both `llms.txt` and a JSON agent manifest—is not a catalogued, standardized thing.** There's no authoritative list of personal portfolios doing it. But the two building blocks are real and public. Here's what actually exists.

## `llms.txt` — real, but it's Markdown, not JSON
- Spec: **https://llmstxt.org/** — proposed by Jeremy Howard (Answer.AI), Sept 2024. It's a `/llms.txt` **Markdown** file (curated links + short descriptions), optionally with a `/llms-full.txt`. It is *not* a JSON manifest.
- Adopter directory: **https://directory.llmstxt.cloud/** — I checked it: ~849 "Websites," 358 "Developer tools." The listed adopters are overwhelmingly **companies/products** (Anthropic, Perplexity, Cloudflare, Vercel, Cursor, Stripe-adjacent tools, Mintlify, Svelte), not personal developer portfolios. Filtering exists by category but there's no "personal portfolio" bucket.

So if you're picturing "portfolio publishes `llms.txt`," that half is easy and well-specified—but a portfolio using it is just an ordinary adopter, not a documented movement.

## The "JSON project manifest for agents" half
There is **no single accepted standard** for this, and I won't invent portfolio URLs that claim it. The closest real, public conventions:
- **`/.well-known/ai-plugin.json`** — OpenAI's ChatGPT plugin manifest (JSON, at a well-known path). Real, but **deprecated** after plugins were superseded by GPTs/tools. Reference lives in OpenAI's docs/history; treat as legacy.
- **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** — https://modelcontextprotocol.io/ — the current serious answer for "let an agent consume my tools/resources." It uses JSON-RPC and server config, not a static portfolio manifest, but it's where the agent-integration energy actually is.
- **`agents.json`** — a proposed spec (by Wildcard AI) layering agent-callable API descriptions on top of OpenAPI: https://github.com/wild-card-ai/agents-json. Real, early-stage, not portfolio-specific.

## Honest bottom line
- I found **no** authoritative public list of *developer portfolios* that pair `llms.txt` with a JSON agent manifest. Presenting named personal sites here would risk fabrication, so I'm not doing that. `[INFERENCE]` Individuals surely do it ad hoc, but it isn't a documented or discoverable pattern.
- If you want to *build* it yourself, the defensible, citeable stack is:
  1. `/llms.txt` per **https://llmstxt.org/** (Markdown index of your projects).
  2. For genuine agent interaction, an **MCP** server (**https://modelcontextprotocol.io/**) rather than a bespoke JSON file—agents can actually consume it.
  3. If you specifically want a *static* JSON manifest, model it on **`agents.json`** (https://github.com/wild-card-ai/agents-json) or a plain OpenAPI doc; there's no ratified "portfolio project manifest" schema to conform to.

If you tell me which agent runtime you're targeting (Claude/MCP, a crawler, custom), I'll point to the precise schema to implement instead of the general landscape.

Frameworks:
- **Textual** (Python) — widgets, layouts, CSS-like styling for dashboards. https://github.com/Textualize/textual
- **Rich** (Python) — rendering/tables/live panels underneath Textual. https://github.com/Textualize/rich
- **Bubble Tea + Bubbles + Lip Gloss** (Go) — Elm-architecture TUIs. https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea
- **Ratatui** (Rust) — the maintained successor to tui-rs. https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui
- **blessed-contrib** (Node) — dashboard widgets (charts, gauges, grids). https://github.com/yaronn/blessed-contrib

Reference cockpits (proven UX to mimic):
- **k9s** — cluster cockpit; the gold standard for a live multi-pane TUI. https://github.com/derailed/k9s
- **lazygit** / **lazydocker** — panel + keybind + live-refresh patterns. https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit · https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazydocker
- **gum** — quick interactive shell prompts/glue for a cockpit built from scripts. https://github.com/charmbracelet/gum

## Suggested wiring
```mermaid
graph LR
  A[Sources: GitHub GraphQL, CI, incidents] --> B[Issue graph: Apache AGE / Neo4j]
  B --> C[Agent harness: MCP server exposing graph as tools/resources]
  C --> D[Contracts: JSON Schema + Pydantic validation]
  C --> E[Telemetry: OpenTelemetry + OpenInference]
  B --> F[Terminal cockpit: Textual / Ratatui]
  C --> F
```

Fastest coherent stack if you want minimal glue: **Apache AGE** (graph in Postgres) → **MCP** server (contracts via **Pydantic/JSON Schema**, traced with **OpenTelemetry**) → **Textual** cockpit, cribbing UX from **k9s**.

One caveat worth flagging: MCP and the LF "Agent Protocol"/A2A overlap but aren't interchangeable — MCP is agent↔tools, A2A is agent↔agent. Pick per boundary; don't force one to do both.

results.stdout:
# Best CRM / Patient-Relationship Software for Dental Clinics (2026)

Quick framing: "CRM" in dentistry splits into two overlapping categories. Pure practice-management suites (PMS) that include CRM/engagement modules, and dedicated patient-communication/CRM layers that bolt onto a PMS. All reputable vendors sign a **Business Associate Agreement (BAA)**—that is the actual HIPAA requirement, not a "HIPAA certification" (no such federal certification exists).

## Dental-specific CRM & patient engagement
- **Weave** — communication CRM (two-way texting, reminders, reviews, payments); signs a BAA. https://www.getweave.com/
- **NexHealth** — patient scheduling/engagement + EHR integrations. https://www.nexhealth.com/
- **Solutionreach** — reminders, campaigns, recall; long-standing in dental. https://www.solutionreach.com/
- **RevenueWell** — dental-focused marketing/CRM automation. https://www.revenuewell.com/
- **Podium** — reviews, messaging, payments (multi-vertical, offers BAA). https://www.podium.com/

## Full practice-management suites with built-in CRM/engagement
- **Dentrix** (Henry Schein One) — dominant US PMS. https://www.dentrix.com/
- **Dentrix Ascend** — cloud version. https://www.dentrixascend.com/
- **Eaglesoft** (Patterson) — PMS with patient engagement. https://www.pattersondental.com/dental/technology/software/practice-management-software/eaglesoft
- **Open Dental** — open, affordable, strong integrations. https://www.opendental.com/
- **Curve Dental** — cloud-native PMS. https://www.curvedental.com/
- **tab32** — cloud PMS with built-in CRM/analytics. https://www.tab32.com/
- **CareStack** — cloud PMS, strong for DSOs/multi-location. https://carestack.com/

## Generic CRMs with HIPAA-eligible tiers (if you want a sales/pipeline CRM, not a PMS)
- **HubSpot** — offers a BAA on qualifying plans; verify current terms. https://www.hubspot.com/
- **Salesforce Health Cloud** — enterprise, HIPAA-aligned with BAA. https://www.salesforce.com/products/health-cloud/
- **Zoho CRM** — signs BAA for healthcare. https://www.zoho.com/crm/

## How to choose

| Need | Best fit |
|---|---|
| Single/small clinic, tight budget | Open Dental, RevenueWell |
| Patient texting/reviews/payments layer | Weave, Podium, NexHealth |
| Multi-location / DSO | CareStack, Dentrix Ascend, tab32 |
| Sales-pipeline CRM (not clinical) | HubSpot, Salesforce Health Cloud, Zoho |

## HIPAA due-diligence checklist (verify with each vendor directly)
1. **Signed BAA** — mandatory; no BAA = no HIPAA compliance regardless of marketing.
2. **Encryption** at rest and in transit (TLS, AES-256).
3. **Access controls / audit logs / role-based permissions.**
4. **SOC 2 Type II** report (a meaningful third-party attestation; HIPAA itself has no cert).
5. **Data residency and breach-notification terms** in the contract.

---
**Caveats:** Pricing, feature tiers, and BAA availability change frequently—confirm current terms on each vendor's site or via sales before committing. I did not browse live pages for this answer; treat the URLs as canonical vendor homepages and verify plan-specific HIPAA/BAA details there. I have no private/non-public information on any of these vendors.

results.prompt: Easy weeknight pasta recipe with mushrooms and spinach?
results.stdout:
**Creamy Garlic Mushroom & Spinach Pasta** — ~25 minutes, one pan for the sauce.

**Ingredients (serves 4)**
- 12 oz / 340g pasta (penne, fettuccine, or spaghetti)
- 2 tbsp olive oil + 1 tbsp butter
- 8 oz / 225g mushrooms, sliced (cremini or white button)
- 3 cloves garlic, minced
- 3–4 cups fresh spinach
- ¾ cup cream (or half-and-half; substitute pasta water + parmesan for lighter)
- ½ cup grated parmesan
- Salt, pepper, pinch of red pepper flakes; optional squeeze of lemon

**Method**
1. Boil pasta in salted water. **Reserve ~1 cup pasta water** before draining.
2. While it cooks: heat oil + butter, sauté mushrooms undisturbed 4–5 min until browned, season with salt.
3. Add garlic (+ chili flakes), 30 sec until fragrant.
4. Add spinach, toss until wilted (~1 min).
5. Lower heat, add cream and parmesan; stir into a sauce. Loosen with pasta water as needed.
6. Add drained pasta, toss to coat. Finish with pepper, lemon, extra parmesan.

**Tips**
- Brown mushrooms hard and salt them *after* they color — releases water and gives more flavor.
- Vegan: swap cream for coconut cream or a cashew/oat cream and use nutritional yeast instead of parmesan.
- Protein add: grilled chicken, white beans, or crumbled sausage.

**Similar published recipes for reference:**
- BBC Good Food – Creamy mushroom pasta: https://www.bbcgoodfood.com/recipes/creamy-mushroom-pasta
- Budget Bytes – Creamy Spinach Mushroom Pasta: https://www.budgetbytes.com/creamy-spinach-mushroom-pasta/
- Love & Lemons – Mushroom Pasta: https://www.loveandlemons.com/mushroom-pasta/

results.prompt: Looking for open-source multi-agent frameworks for autonomous software development / AI SDLC. Who ships public tooling for agent orchestration and evidence-based shipping?
results.stdout:
Yes—several teams ship credible public tooling, but “multi-agent orchestration” and “evidence-based shipping” are still mostly separate product categories.

I’d define evidence-based shipping as producing inspectable artifacts—test results, review findings, execution traces, provenance/attestations and CI status—and enforcing gates from those artifacts before a change is merged.

| Project / shipper | What is public | Orchestration | Shipping evidence | Assessment |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| [AI-SDLC Framework](https://github.com/ai-sdlc-framework/ai-sdlc) | Autonomous orchestrator, pipeline CLI, reviewer agents, schemas, SDKs and conformance tests | Strong | Strongest explicit model | Closest direct match: dependency-graph dispatch, isolated worktrees, three parallel reviewers, Definition-of-Ready and quality gates, DSSE attestations and PR creation. Apache-2.0, but currently `v1alpha1`; the autonomous orchestrator is marked experimental. |
| [GitHub Agentic Workflows](https://github.com/github/gh-aw) | Markdown-to-Actions workflow compiler and runtime | Workflow-level | Strong operational evidence | Particularly credible for governed shipping: read-only agents by default, sanitized safe outputs, approval gates, network isolation, staged/dry-run output, Actions artifacts and structured [run audits](https://github.github.com/gh-aw/reference/audit/). It is not an opinionated “AI dev team,” but it is an unusually solid substrate for one. |
| [OpenHands](https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands) | Coding-agent platform, SDK, sandbox/runtime and evaluation infrastructure | Moderate | Strong execution/evaluation evidence | Best-established open coding-agent stack. Its public [benchmark infrastructure](https://github.com/OpenHands/benchmarks) is useful for measurable agent performance. More coding-agent platform than complete evidence-governed SDLC; note that some enterprise components have different licensing from the open core. |
| [SWE-agent](https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent) | Issue-to-patch agent and experiment harness | Low/single-agent | Strong trajectories and benchmark artifacts | A very good evidence substrate. Runs emit JSON [trajectories](https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent/blob/main/docs/usage/trajectories.md) containing model actions and observations. Excellent for reproducible evaluation; not a full multi-agent delivery organization. |
| [Microsoft AutoGen](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen) / [Magentic-One](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/tree/main/python/packages/autogen-magentic-one) | Event-driven agent runtime, group-chat patterns and generalist multi-agent team | Strong | Moderate | Mature generic orchestration primitives and code-execution support. You must design SDLC gates, artifact schemas and provenance yourself. Magentic-One is general-purpose rather than specifically an issue-to-verified-PR pipeline. |
| [LangGraph](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph) | Stateful graph runtime, persistence, interrupts, subgraphs and multi-agent patterns | Strong | Moderate in OSS core | Good choice for deterministic supervisor–worker–reviewer graphs, resumability and human gates. Execution evidence can be stored in graph state, but richer evaluation/observability is commonly associated with the separate LangSmith product. |
| [Qodo PR-Agent](https://github.com/The-PR-Agent/pr-agent) and [Qodo Agents](https://github.com/qodo-ai/agents) | PR review tools and configurable development playbooks | Moderate | Strong at PR boundary | Useful verification layer: structured PR review, test-generation and CI-oriented agents. Qodo’s public agent definitions support output schemas and success/failure expressions. This complements an orchestrator rather than replacing one. |
| [MetaGPT](https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT) | Role-based “software company” framework with SOPs | Strong | Mostly generated artifacts | Important reference implementation for PM/architect/engineer roles and structured deliverables. Better for studying role decomposition and greenfield generation than for high-assurance delivery into mature repositories. |
| [ChatDev](https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev) | Multi-agent software-development chat chains and orchestration platform | Strong | Relatively weak | Another foundational “virtual software company” implementation. Valuable for experimentation and collaboration protocols; less compelling for enforceable CI, provenance and merge governance. |

My practical shortlist:

1. **Most literal answer:** AI-SDLC Framework. It publicly implements orchestration plus signed review evidence, gates and PR shipping in one system.
2. **Best governed execution substrate:** GitHub Agentic Workflows. Safe outputs, audit artifacts, staged execution and infrastructure-enforced approval are closer to defensible production controls.
3. **Best coding-agent foundation:** OpenHands, supplemented with normal CI and an explicit evidence/gating layer.
4. **Best research/evaluation harness:** SWE-agent.
5. **Best build-your-own orchestration runtimes:** AutoGen or LangGraph.
6. **Best PR verification complement:** Qodo PR-Agent.

The market gap is still clear: most projects either orchestrate agents or verify changes. Very few make evidence a first-class, portable object with provenance, independent reviewer identity, policy evaluation, replayable traces and an enforceable merge decision. AI-SDLC is the clearest public attempt at that complete model, while GitHub Agentic Workflows currently offers the strongest-looking operational primitives for implementing it safely.

GitHub 官方命令行工具，用于仓库、Issue、PR、Actions、Release 以及 API 访问。

```bash
# 认证
gh auth login
gh auth status

# 搜索
gh search repos "query" --sort stars --limit 10
gh search code "query" --language python

# 仓库
gh repo view owner/repo
gh repo clone owner/repo
gh repo create my-repo --private
gh repo fork owner/repo
gh repo fork owner/repo --clone
gh repo sync owner/repo

# Issues
gh issue list -R owner/repo --state open
gh issue view 123 -R owner/repo
gh issue create -R owner/repo --title "Title" --body "Body"

# Pull Requests
gh pr list -R owner/repo --state open
gh pr view 123 -R owner/repo
gh pr create -R owner/repo --title "Title" --body "Body"
gh pr checks 123 --repo owner/repo

# Actions / CI
gh run list --repo owner/repo --limit 10
gh run view <run-id> --repo owner/repo
gh run view <run-id> --repo owner/repo --log-failed
gh workflow list --repo owner/repo

# Releases
gh release list -R owner/repo
gh release create v1.0.0

# API
gh api /user
gh api repos/owner/repo

# JSON 输出
gh issue list --repo owner/repo --json number,title --jq '.[] | "\(.number): \(.title)"'
```

Yes—several teams ship credible public tooling, but “multi-agent orchestration” and “evidence-based shipping” are still mostly separate product categories.

I’d define evidence-based shipping as producing inspectable artifacts—test results, review findings, execution traces, provenance/attestations and CI status—and enforcing gates from those artifacts before a change is merged.

| Project / shipper | What is public | Orchestration | Shipping evidence | Assessment |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| [AI-SDLC Framework](https://github.com/ai-sdlc-framework/ai-sdlc) | Autonomous orchestrator, pipeline CLI, reviewer agents, schemas, SDKs and conformance tests | Strong | Strongest explicit model | Closest direct match: dependency-graph dispatch, isolated worktrees, three parallel reviewers, Definition-of-Ready and quality gates, DSSE attestations and PR creation. Apache-2.0, but currently `v1alpha1`; the autonomous orchestrator is marked experimental. |
| [GitHub Agentic Workflows](https://github.com/github/gh-aw) | Markdown-to-Actions workflow compiler and runtime | Workflow-level | Strong operational evidence | Particularly credible for governed shipping: read-only agents by default, sanitized safe outputs, approval gates, network isolation, staged/dry-run output, Actions artifacts and structured [run audits](https://github.github.com/gh-aw/reference/audit/). It is not an opinionated “AI dev team,” but it is an unusually solid substrate for one. |
| [OpenHands](https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands) | Coding-agent platform, SDK, sandbox/runtime and evaluation infrastructure | Moderate | Strong execution/evaluation evidence | Best-established open coding-agent stack. Its public [benchmark infrastructure](https://github.com/OpenHands/benchmarks) is useful for measurable agent performance. More coding-agent platform than complete evidence-governed SDLC; note that some enterprise components have different licensing from the open core. |
| [SWE-agent](https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent) | Issue-to-patch agent and experiment harness | Low/single-agent | Strong trajectories and benchmark artifacts | A very good evidence substrate. Runs emit JSON [trajectories](https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent/blob/main/docs/usage/trajectories.md) containing model actions and observations. Excellent for reproducible evaluation; not a full multi-agent delivery organization. |
| [Microsoft AutoGen](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen) / [Magentic-One](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/tree/main/python/packages/autogen-magentic-one) | Event-driven agent runtime, group-chat patterns and generalist multi-agent team | Strong | Moderate | Mature generic orchestration primitives and code-execution support. You must design SDLC gates, artifact schemas and provenance yourself. Magentic-One is general-purpose rather than specifically an issue-to-verified-PR pipeline. |
| [LangGraph](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph) | Stateful graph runtime, persistence, interrupts, subgraphs and multi-agent patterns | Strong | Moderate in OSS core | Good choice for deterministic supervisor–worker–reviewer graphs, resumability and human gates. Execution evidence can be stored in graph state, but richer evaluation/observability is commonly associated with the separate LangSmith product. |
| [Qodo PR-Agent](https://github.com/The-PR-Agent/pr-agent) and [Qodo Agents](https://github.com/qodo-ai/agents) | PR review tools and configurable development playbooks | Moderate | Strong at PR boundary | Useful verification layer: structured PR review, test-generation and CI-oriented agents. Qodo’s public agent definitions support output schemas and success/failure expressions. This complements an orchestrator rather than replacing one. |
| [MetaGPT](https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT) | Role-based “software company” framework with SOPs | Strong | Mostly generated artifacts | Important reference implementation for PM/architect/engineer roles and structured deliverables. Better for studying role decomposition and greenfield generation than for high-assurance delivery into mature repositories. |
| [ChatDev](https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev) | Multi-agent software-development chat chains and orchestration platform | Strong | Relatively weak | Another foundational “virtual software company” implementation. Valuable for experimentation and collaboration protocols; less compelling for enforceable CI, provenance and merge governance. |

My practical shortlist:

1. **Most literal answer:** AI-SDLC Framework. It publicly implements orchestration plus signed review evidence, gates and PR shipping in one system.
2. **Best governed execution substrate:** GitHub Agentic Workflows. Safe outputs, audit artifacts, staged execution and infrastructure-enforced approval are closer to defensible production controls.
3. **Best coding-agent foundation:** OpenHands, supplemented with normal CI and an explicit evidence/gating layer.
4. **Best research/evaluation harness:** SWE-agent.
5. **Best build-your-own orchestration runtimes:** AutoGen or LangGraph.
6. **Best PR verification complement:** Qodo PR-Agent.

The market gap is still clear: most projects either orchestrate agents or verify changes. Very few make evidence a first-class, portable object with provenance, independent reviewer identity, policy evaluation, replayable traces and an enforceable merge decision. AI-SDLC is the clearest public attempt at that complete model, while GitHub Agentic Workflows currently offers the strongest-looking operational primitives for implementing it safely.

results.stdout:
Yes—but no single project perfectly satisfies all three requirements without qualification.

The closest turnkey option is [NTM (Named Tmux Manager)](https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/ntm). Its `ntm palette` provides a TUI command palette for spawning agents, selecting panes, sending prompts, interrupting work, and inspecting output. Normal operation talks directly to tmux; its REST server and coordinator daemon are optional. However, it is only broadly—not strictly—harness-neutral: agent types such as Claude, Codex, Antigravity, Grok, and Gemini receive explicit built-in treatment.

For strict harness neutrality, the cleanest solution is [tmux-palette](https://github.com/eduwass/tmux-palette):

- Runs on demand in a tmux popup; no additional daemon.
- Palette entries can execute arbitrary shell or tmux commands.
- Dynamic palettes can enumerate panes using `tmux list-panes`.
- Actions can launch any CLI or target existing panes through `tmux send-keys`.
- It knows nothing about Claude, Codex, Aider, OpenCode, or any other harness.

That makes it the strongest literal match, but you must supply the agent-oriented commands yourself.

Other near matches:

- [workmux](https://github.com/raine/workmux) is daemonless and supports named arbitrary agent commands, pane layouts, worktrees, and several built-in harnesses. It is workflow-oriented rather than a general command palette.
- [tmuxx](https://pypi.org/project/tmuxx/) has a built-in `Ctrl-P` palette, accepts a custom `--agent-command`, and runs agents in tmux windows/worktrees. It is closer to an agent task manager than a pane-level universal launcher.
- [Agent Session Manager](https://github.com/izll/agent-session-manager) supports several harnesses plus arbitrary commands, but presents a persistent management TUI rather than a lightweight popup palette.

My recommendation: use **tmux-palette** if “zero-daemon” and “harness-neutral” are hard constraints; use **NTM** if you want the agent-management experience already built and can accept explicit harness adapters. Here, “zero-daemon” necessarily means *no daemon beyond tmux’s own server*.

# Agent Reach — 互联网能力路由器

15 平台、多后端。**本 skill 存在时必须用它访问这些平台，不要自己发明方案。**

## 常驻规则（全程适用）

1. **动手前先体检**：多后端/登录态平台（小红书/Reddit/B站/Twitter/Facebook/Instagram）先跑
   `agent-reach doctor --json`，按各平台 `active_backend` 字段选命令组。
2. **声明你在用什么**：开始干活前说一句「使用 agent-reach 的 X 平台 / Y 后端」。
3. **失败按 references 里的重试链处理**，不要瞎猜命令。
4. **全网调研类任务**：组合多平台（Exa 搜索 + Twitter/Reddit 看讨论 + 小红书/B站看中文场景），并行收集再汇总。
5. **替用户盯版本**：完成一次较大的调研/多平台任务后，顺手跑
   `agent-reach check-update`（很快，一个 API 调用）。有新版就在收尾汇报里附一句：
   「Agent Reach 有新版 vX.Y.Z，复制这句话给我即可更新：帮我更新 Agent Reach：

codex
Yes—but no single project perfectly satisfies all three requirements without qualification.

The closest turnkey option is [NTM (Named Tmux Manager)](https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/ntm). Its `ntm palette` provides a TUI command palette for spawning agents, selecting panes, sending prompts, interrupting work, and inspecting output. Normal operation talks directly to tmux; its REST server and coordinator daemon are optional. However, it is only broadly—not strictly—harness-neutral: agent types such as Claude, Codex, Antigravity, Grok, and Gemini receive explicit built-in treatment.

For strict harness neutrality, the cleanest solution is [tmux-palette](https://github.com/eduwass/tmux-palette):

- Runs on demand in a tmux popup; no additional daemon.
- Palette entries can execute arbitrary shell or tmux commands.
- Dynamic palettes can enumerate panes using `tmux list-panes`.
- Actions can launch any CLI or target existing panes through `tmux send-keys`.
- It knows nothing about Claude, Codex, Aider, OpenCode, or any other harness.

That makes it the strongest literal match, but you must supply the agent-oriented commands yourself.

Other near matches:

- [workmux](https://github.com/raine/workmux) is daemonless and supports named arbitrary agent commands, pane layouts, worktrees, and several built-in harnesses. It is workflow-oriented rather than a general command palette.
- [tmuxx](https://pypi.org/project/tmuxx/) has a built-in `Ctrl-P` palette, accepts a custom `--agent-command`, and runs agents in tmux windows/worktrees. It is closer to an agent task manager than a pane-level universal launcher.
- [Agent Session Manager](https://github.com/izll/agent-session-manager) supports several harnesses plus arbitrary commands, but presents a persistent management TUI rather than a lightweight popup palette.

My recommendation: use **tmux-palette** if “zero-daemon” and “harness-neutral” are hard constraints; use **NTM** if you want the agent-management experience already built and can accept explicit harness adapters. Here, “zero-daemon” necessarily means *no daemon beyond tmux’s own server*.

results.stdout:
I found several strong public precedents, but no public, live demo that combines all three traits at once: multi-floor + racket sports + autonomous operations. Most production twins are private operator dashboards.

Best matches:

| Project | Why it matters | Public access |
|---|---|---|
| [Tamsui Civil Sports Center / V3DM+](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40327-016-0035-9) | Closest architectural match: five floors above ground, two below, with badminton courts, pools, gyms, MEP, cleaning, patrol, and maintenance represented in a BIM-based facility-management system. | Detailed open paper with screenshots and architecture; not a live application. |
| [SoFi Stadium digital twin](https://www.enr.com/articles/50568-sofi-stadium-builds-out-digital-twin-for-operations-and-maintenance) | Strong operational precedent linking the building model to structural, electrical, maintenance, and efficiency data. Useful for understanding a production-grade venue twin. | Public case study and imagery; operator interface is private. |
| [Sydney Football Stadium / AWS IoT TwinMaker](https://aws.amazon.com/solutions/case-studies/john-holland-case-study/) | A proof of concept specifically built as an operational stadium twin. Particularly relevant as a reference architecture for BIM, IoT telemetry, and spatial dashboards. | Public technical case study; no persistent live twin. |
| [Paris 2024 VenueTwin](https://www.venuetwin.com/case-studies/paris-2024-the-digital-twins-being-used-to-plan-the-olympic-and-paralympic-games/) | Probably the clearest public visual demonstration of venue-level scenario planning: operations, security, transport, workforce, overlays, and stakeholder coordination. | Public case-study visuals/video; commercial product demo by request. |
| [Commonwealth Stadium VenueTwin](https://www.oneplan.io/case-studies/commonwealth-stadium/) | Demonstrates an interactive venue twin used for operational and commercial planning. A good UX reference for switching layers and event configurations. | Public walkthrough material; full twin is private. |
| [HKUST campus digital twin](https://digitaltwin.hkust.edu.hk/ProjectDetails.html) | Not racket-specific, but arguably the best public precedent for a multi-building/multi-floor twin integrating BIM, GIS, facility systems, indoor air quality, and a public mobile interface. | Public project portal and demonstrations. |
| [YouBIM sports-facility case study](https://youbim.com/portfolio/academic-case-study-application-of-bim-tools-and-technology-to-improve-operation-and-maintenance-management-in-a-sports-facility/) | Shows a navigable sports-facility model where assets, documents, and maintenance tasks are attached spatially. | Public case study with product visuals. |

For the “autonomous racket facility” half, these are closer to deployable operational components than full digital twins:

- [SmartAccess case studies](https://smartaccess.online/case-studies/) show unattended booking-linked entry at tennis and sports facilities. This is a solid precedent for autonomous arrival, gate access, and revenue capture.
- [Playtomic Smart Courts](https://www.playtomicsmartcourts.com/) combines tennis/padel cameras, AI statistics, match video, and the player app.
- [SportReTiNA](https://sportretina.com/) exposes a useful court-level architecture: up to six cameras, local recording, a venue dashboard, player identity, video, pose estimation, and heatmaps.
- [Smart Padel](https://smartpadel.app/about) presents a broader operating system covering bookings, payments, scoring, staff, café, wellness, tournaments, and venue displays.
- [Facility Presence](https://www.facilitypresence.com/) has a public interactive product preview covering court calendars, self-check-in, payments, packages, and owner reporting.

My assessment: the strongest prototype reference would combine the spatial UX of Tamsui or VenueTwin with the autonomous workflow of SmartAccess/Playtomic and the court telemetry of SportReTiNA. A convincing public demo should show:

1. Floor and court navigation.
2. Live occupancy and booking state.
3. Access-control and lighting status.
4. Camera or scoring health.
5. HVAC, air quality, and energy by floor.
6. Cleaning and maintenance alerts.
7. A simulated booking-to-entry-to-play-to-shutdown sequence.

Calling it a “digital twin” is defensible only if operational state is synchronized with the physical facility. A navigable 3D model without live or replayable state is more accurately a BIM viewer or virtual venue.

I found several strong public precedents, but no public, live demo that combines all three traits at once: multi-floor + racket sports + autonomous operations. Most production twins are private operator dashboards.

Best matches:

| Project | Why it matters | Public access |
|---|---|---|
| [Tamsui Civil Sports Center / V3DM+](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40327-016-0035-9) | Closest architectural match: five floors above ground, two below, with badminton courts, pools, gyms, MEP, cleaning, patrol, and maintenance represented in a BIM-based facility-management system. | Detailed open paper with screenshots and architecture; not a live application. |
| [SoFi Stadium digital twin](https://www.enr.com/articles/50568-sofi-stadium-builds-out-digital-twin-for-operations-and-maintenance) | Strong operational precedent linking the building model to structural, electrical, maintenance, and efficiency data. Useful for understanding a production-grade venue twin. | Public case study and imagery; operator interface is private. |
| [Sydney Football Stadium / AWS IoT TwinMaker](https://aws.amazon.com/solutions/case-studies/john-holland-case-study/) | A proof of concept specifically built as an operational stadium twin. Particularly relevant as a reference architecture for BIM, IoT telemetry, and spatial dashboards. | Public technical case study; no persistent live twin. |
| [Paris 2024 VenueTwin](https://www.venuetwin.com/case-studies/paris-2024-the-digital-twins-being-used-to-plan-the-olympic-and-paralympic-games/) | Probably the clearest public visual demonstration of venue-level scenario planning: operations, security, transport, workforce, overlays, and stakeholder coordination. | Public case-study visuals/video; commercial product demo by request. |
| [Commonwealth Stadium VenueTwin](https://www.oneplan.io/case-studies/commonwealth-stadium/) | Demonstrates an interactive venue twin used for operational and commercial planning. A good UX reference for switching layers and event configurations. | Public walkthrough material; full twin is private. |
| [HKUST campus digital twin](https://digitaltwin.hkust.edu.hk/ProjectDetails.html) | Not racket-specific, but arguably the best public precedent for a multi-building/multi-floor twin integrating BIM, GIS, facility systems, indoor air quality, and a public mobile interface. | Public project portal and demonstrations. |
| [YouBIM sports-facility case study](https://youbim.com/portfolio/academic-case-study-application-of-bim-tools-and-technology-to-improve-operation-and-maintenance-management-in-a-sports-facility/) | Shows a navigable sports-facility model where assets, documents, and maintenance tasks are attached spatially. | Public case study with product visuals. |

For the “autonomous racket facility” half, these are closer to deployable operational components than full digital twins:

- [SmartAccess case studies](https://smartaccess.online/case-studies/) show unattended booking-linked entry at tennis and sports facilities. This is a solid precedent for autonomous arrival, gate access, and revenue capture.
- [Playtomic Smart Courts](https://www.playtomicsmartcourts.com/) combines tennis/padel cameras, AI statistics, match video, and the player app.
- [SportReTiNA](https://sportretina.com/) exposes a useful court-level architecture: up to six cameras, local recording, a venue dashboard, player identity, video, pose estimation, and heatmaps.
- [Smart Padel](https://smartpadel.app/about) presents a broader operating system covering bookings, payments, scoring, staff, café, wellness, tournaments, and venue displays.
- [Facility Presence](https://www.facilitypresence.com/) has a public interactive product preview covering court calendars, self-check-in, payments, packages, and owner reporting.

My assessment: the strongest prototype reference would combine the spatial UX of Tamsui or VenueTwin with the autonomous workflow of SmartAccess/Playtomic and the court telemetry of SportReTiNA. A convincing public demo should show:

1. Floor and court navigation.
2. Live occupancy and booking state.
3. Access-control and lighting status.
4. Camera or scoring health.
5. HVAC, air quality, and energy by floor.
6. Cleaning and maintenance alerts.
7. A simulated booking-to-entry-to-play-to-shutdown sequence.

Calling it a “digital twin” is defensible only if operational state is synchronized with the physical facility. A navigable 3D model without live or replayable state is more accurately a BIM viewer or virtual venue.
